waterbodies.name: Manila Bay
waterbodies.scopeNote: One shared bay identity. The 2014-2015 NFRDI survey defines a Cavite stratum, but its station map has not been georeferenced. A 2020 NFRDI annual-report summary describes landed catch across eight Manila Bay sites and reports Sardinella fimbriata as 19% of the aggregate; it does not assign that taxon to Rosario Fish Port or a capture station. Neither source establishes current species presence, current bay boundaries, or municipal-water geometry. A Marine Regions named-bay polygon was used only for an exploratory OBIS query and is not an official or app boundary. A CC BY 4.0 National Museum specimen archive and its GBIF index yielded seven historical rows with sourceStateProvince=Cavite, but all seven omit locality and waterBody. The dataset description includes landing-site, market, port and nearby-sea contexts without per-record capture-origin rules, so these records are not assigned to Manila Bay or another Cavite waterbody. A 2021 EMB Island C EIS also reports a 17-row fishing-ground table (15 fish-labeled and two invertebrate rows) covering Rosario, Noveleta, and Cavite City near a proposed Manila Bay reclamation project. It is linked here only as broad historical Cavite-side bay context: row-level localities and item-specific reuse terms remain unresolved, no table names were transcribed into this repository, and no fish occurrence or whole-bay distribution is inferred. A separate official 2021 Avalar seabed-dredging EISR has indexed records of marine-ecology field documentation on 20 and 22 May and a broad fishery list spanning Cavite-side Manila Bay grounds. Its field table combines actual swimming-crab catch records with interview-based fish context; the broader fish list is not attributed by taxon to a station or municipality. Direct PDF access returned 403, item-specific reuse terms are unresolved, and the source may overlap nearby EIS evidence. It is linked only as historical shared-bay context; no species row or public claim is inferred. A separate dated GBIF-indexed USNM preserved-specimen record reports Stolephorus celsior from “Manila Bay, Naic, Cavite” with waterBody “North Pacific Ocean, Manila Bay” and no coordinates. It is retained as one historical, source-reported association with shared Manila Bay only; the Smithsonian record interface returned its JavaScript shell, so the physical catalog label was not independently checked. The primary species description confirms the Manila Bay taxon context and Rosario type locality but does not mention USNM 204231 or Naic. Do not transfer this record to Palanas River, infer current presence, or publish it as a current fishing recommendation.

waterbodies.name: Maragondon River
waterbodies.scopeNote: River identity only; monitored segments do not delimit the entire channel or sanctuary. A 2014 goby barcoding paper is a historical fish lead, but it reports conflicting putative species identities and has no adopted reach geometry; all three species-level claims remain held for independent review. GBIF's exact Maragondon River query returned zero rows, which does not establish fish absence. The DENR-BMB 2016 Atlas Annex 2b also lists this river under Cavite and reports multiple municipalities; these are source-era locality context only and do not delimit the channel. A 2024 primary study reports 48 juvenile Tilapia sp. sampled at upstream, midstream, and downstream Maragondon River stations in April 2023. The authors withheld species resolution due to possible hybridization and gene-pool uncertainty; this is genus-level historical evidence only. It does not establish current presence, catchability, full-river coverage, salinity, or geometry. A 2018 sampling study published in 2019 labels fish samples Oreochromis niloticus, but this review found no independently verifiable specimen identifier or diagnostic identification protocol and no item-specific reuse license. A 2024 study reports Tilapia sp. and withholds species resolution; keep the earlier species-level claim held and do not resolve it to O. niloticus. DENR-EMB CALABARZON indexed monitoring information reports that Maragondon River was included in monitoring in 2018 and that its first-half 2020 sampling was conducted in January and February; the indexed source lists Class C. Exact station locations, measurements, and a link between any station and Gapan/Sapang were unavailable. This is historical water-quality context only, not current safety, fish evidence, or channel geometry. The 2024 provincial profile reports a 35.6 km source-described river route and Manila Bay/Ternate receiving context; this is not a surveyed channel trace or fish evidence.

waterbodies.name: Maragondon River Estuary
waterbodies.scopeNote: Primary project site name; exact tidal reach and salinity need review. Do not reuse a management-site area as the wetted estuary. A 2022 SCS SAP Project evaluation names the Maragondon River Estuary and reports planned Ternate Marine Park biodiversity monitoring at four stations twice yearly, with BAMS every three years. The report provides no monitoring outputs, fish taxa, station coordinates, or estuary geometry; its 35,700 ha mouth-MPA figure is not adopted. A bounded public web-index search on 2026-10-31 did not locate a completed BMS/BAMS fish-results report explicitly tied to this estuary. This is a retrieval gap only, not evidence of fish absence or proof that monitoring was not performed. Keep the Maragondon River Tilapia/goby records separate until a station-to-estuary crosswalk is available.

waterbodies.name: Taal Lake
waterbodies.scopeNote: Freshwater identity context only; no complete fish list, safety or fishing-access approval. The 2021-2022 Sardinella tawilis diet study supports one attributed natural-diet guide for Taal Lake only, not a whole-lake species inventory or presence elsewhere. Three historical CAS preserved-specimen records dated 1931 and 2011 provide explicit Lake Taal and source-locality text for three species-level assertions; CONTINENT_INVALID flags are retained and coordinates are withheld. These records do not establish current presence or a complete inventory. Mutia et al. (2025) review historical Midas cichlid landed catches, but its CC BY-NC 4.0 scope and eight-versus-nine municipality mismatch remain held; no catch or municipal-presence claim is projected. A 2026-10-24 exact-field screen of four queries in the CC BY 4.0 National Museum GBIF dataset returned zero; this bounded discovery result is not evidence of absence. Two additional GBIF coordinate-envelope specimen candidates crosswalk to Taal localities only through FishBase catalog-number matches; missing GBIF locality fields, unresolved institution-code provenance, and FishBase's CC BY-NC 4.0 terms keep both held pending primary-catalog and reuse review. A 2006 UPLB repository abstract and a third-party whole-volume copy provide historical Taal Lake Jaguar Guapote gut-content leads, but the abstract and body give conflicting fish percentages; the official full article, sample details, and reuse terms remain unavailable or unverified, so no public diet guide is admitted.

waterbodies.name: Pansipit River
waterbodies.scopeNote: Four 1933 CC0 Field Museum specimen records support four historical species-locality assertions by exact Pansipit River text. All carry institution/collection quality flags; three also carry recorded-date mismatch flags. Their shared coordinate has no uncertainty and is withheld. No exact reach, estuary, salinity, current presence, or complete river list is inferred. The river links Taal Lake to Balayan Bay; one salinity class cannot be assigned to every reach from this connection. The DENR-BMB 2016 Atlas Annex 2b independently names Pansipit River and lists Lemery, Taal, Agoncillo and San Nicolas; this does not assign salinity to every reach. Mendoza et al. (2015) reports a 2012 juvenile-fish/gut-content study of the upstream lake-river reach; the species/diet table remains held pending rights review, and no diet or current-presence claim is added. Mercene and Alzona (1990) report one Pansipit River fish corral monitored daily from July 1983 to June 1984; its separate table totals 3,148.1 kg across five source-spelled catch groups. This is a historical single-corral landing sample, not a river-wide inventory, current-presence estimate, or estuary record. The separate three-corral Taal Lake table (981.1 kg) is not assigned to the river. The article abstract names Mugil dussumieri, whereas the Pansipit table prints Mugil sp.; retain that discrepancy. A separate WoRMS crosswalk maps binomial names where possible, but does not confirm the original catch identifications; the `Mugil sp.` label remains genus-rank. Reuse review remains pending. Larval/fry samples were collected separately in Balayan Bay 10-15 m from shore near the river mouth and are not crosswalked to the estuary. Corpuz et al. (2016) report a 2011 two-period survey of the Lake Taal inlet and outlet rivers; the official UPLB repository abstract reports 36 species richness in Pansipit River (37 pooled across Pansipit, Looc and Magapi). This is a historical river result, not current presence or a complete present-day inventory, and it is not assigned to the separately modeled estuary. The paper has conflicting individual totals (3,342 in abstract; 3,346 in results), season wording and station/sample denominators; no season-specific assignment or per-station effort is inferred. UKDR/JESAM policy assigns article copyright to UKDR; the species-by-site and feeding-habit table remains untranscribed pending rights review. No species/diet app record is added. Pagulayan and Magbanua (1999) report a monthly beach-seine survey from February through December 1998 at four Pansipit River sites and one separate Palanas River site. Their proceedings abstract reports 33 species for Pansipit (21 exclusive and 12 shared with Palanas), historical aggregate only. Species names remain untranscribed because the proceedings front matter requires prior permission for reproduction; no current presence or Pansipit-estuary assignment is inferred.

waterbodies.name: Palanas River
waterbodies.scopeNote: Named as a separate sampling river in Pagulayan and Magbanua (1999); the one-page proceedings abstract reports one Palanas site and a 38-species historical richness aggregate, with 26 taxa exclusive to Palanas and 12 shared with Pansipit. The source describes Palanas as a diverging branch of Pansipit with a separate Balayan Bay outlet about 3 km from the Pansipit mouth. No species names, exact municipality, route, coordinates, salinity, current presence, or validated boundary is established. Do not equate this river with Barangay Palanas or another namesake without an authoritative crosswalk; no species/app row is added. A BFAR-hosted 1947 order separately names Palanas Creek within Lemery and describes tidal waters/tributaries to a Pansipit junction; whether this is the same feature as the 1998 study site is unresolved, and the old order is not current fishing guidance. A 2006 EMB source names another Palanas River (Naic) as a Timalan tributary; that Cavite lead is kept separate.
